segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So again, "you're staying here", let's make that, "you're staying here" informal.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Te quedas aquí. "You're not staying here."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No te quedas aquí. Or acá. Now, if you want to make that a question, "Aren't you staying here?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿No te quedas aquí? "Why aren't you staying here?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was "I go" or "I'm going"? "I'm going on a voyage."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Voy, good. So, how do you think you would say, "I'm going to stay." "I'm going to remain myself."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "Until 7:00." Until 7:00. Seven is siete, similar to the beginning of September.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: September in Spanish actually is either septiembre or setiembre. You have two versions of it in Spanish, septiembre with the p or without the p, setiembre. And you can see how siete is like the beginning sept with the split of the e.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, "I'm going to stay", "I'm going to remain myself until 7:00." "I'm going to stay until 7:00."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Voy a quedarme hasta las siete.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Voy a quedarme hasta las siete. Very good. How do you say, "I want to stay"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quiero quedarme. "Do you want to stay?" Let's talk informally. "Do you want to stay?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, very good. ¿Quieres quedarte? "Do you want to remain yourself?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Debo, good. What is "we owe" or "we must"? And the "to" form is deber, deber, "to owe". So, "we"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "We must stay." So, "we owe to remain ourselves", "we must stay."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Debemos que... darme... eh que... quedarnos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Debemos quedarnos. Of course, this nos or me or te can come at the beginning as well: Nos debemos quedar, debemos quedarnos. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was "I have", in the sense of possession? So not haber, the other have.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tengo. So if we add on que to tengo, we get the meaning of "have to", which is just like debo, but less serious-sounding, just like in English. "I must stay" sounds a little bit more serious than "I have to stay". And that difference in in register, how it feels, is the same in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say, "I have to stay"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And how would you say, "You have to stay", speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tienes que quedarte. Good. "You have to stay here", informally still.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "I want to know why you have to stay here." "I want to know..." First bit, don't think about the whole sentence, just think of "I want".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quiero saber. Now forget that bit. "Why..."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Very good. Quiero saber por qué tienes que quedarte aquí. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was "I can" or "I have the power to"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No puedo quedarme. Do you remember how to say "tonight", or "this night"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Esta noche, good. Uh "I can't stay tonight."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No puedo quedarme esta noche. The "to" form of can is poder, poder. And this o is splitting when we stress it and say puedo, poder. So how would you say "we can" or "we are able"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No podemos quedarnos esta noche. What was "to think", or "to be pensive"? "To think"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, it should be pensas. It split...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, if we want to say, "Do you plan on staying here tonight?", we can just say, "Do you think to stay here tonight?", huh? "Do you think to stay here tonight?" So how would we say this, informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Piensas quedarte aquí esta noche? Very good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now how would you say, "I have stayed." "I have stayed", or "I have remained myself." "I have stayed."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He quedado me... He... me he quedado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And don't want you to guess and see where it feels good, so with logic you want to place it. And if you're wrong, it's fine, because if you got there through a faulted logic you will change the logic through that mistake.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So tell me the rule about where that me can go.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: It goes after the "to" form, and before everything else?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Before the changed verb. It's very important the way we instruct ourselves. Now I'm giving you always the simplest way that we can instruct ourselves accurately. If I tell you "before the verb" and you tell yourself "at the beginning", you lose something, huh? You lose a certain clarity.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Yeah, 'cause nouns might come into the sentence and then...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Exactly. "We have stayed", "we have remained ourselves"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Nos hemos quedado. "We haven't stayed"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. No nos hemos quedado. "You have stayed", informal, "you have stayed"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Te has quedado. Make it a question: "Have you stayed?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And let's be emphatic now. Just say the word for "you".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Tú te has quedado? Let's make it negative now. "Haven't you stayed?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Tú no te has quedado? Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Llamar in Spanish is "to call", or "to phone", "to telephone", llamar. L-L, which we said is pronounced like "y" in most of Spanish-speaking world. "To call"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Llamo. If you want to introduce yourself, instead of saying "my name is", in Spanish it's much more common to say "I call myself".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me llamo. And then you can introduce yourself: Me llamo Mihalis, for example.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "you call yourself", informal?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Te llamas. If you want to ask them their name, you will say "how do you call yourself?", and the word for "how" is cómo, cómo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how do you say, "How do you call yourself?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Cómo te llamas? You might have heard this around and not understood actually how it's being constructed, and now we understand it. It's "how do you call yourself?", ¿Cómo te llamas?
